questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had only been to Prague once, very shortly as a child, and I found it had a lot of interesting culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Prague is a great place to be on exchange, it has a lot of student life for Erasmus students!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Generally everything you needed to know was on their website, so pretty easy. Courses were a bit hectic to figure out though, since the schedules are published at the earliest two weeks before classes start..

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I don't know that I had a lot of assistance, but I was also very prepared and didn't need much help. I had some issues with my name being registered twice in the system (one with 'o' and one with 'ø') which gave some issues with the student card and course registration, and took a lot of pushing from my side to make them figure out what the issue was.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I specifically had some issues with registration, but other than that pretty straight forward. I did hear some of the students from other faculties got more assistance from their faculties than just registration day, which would have been nice.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were a few options for accommodation at the dorms for Erasmus. I stayed at Troja (Kolej 17. listopadu), which I also noted in my application as preferred. All dorms have a double room, so you have a roommate, but at Troja you share kitchen/bathroom only with one other room, instead of one of them being shared with the entire hall. In general the Erasmus students are also gathered together, so you would be living with other internationals at the dorms.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: We had a small shared kitchen. Only two hot plates, and a not that big fridge, but we managed. For bigger cooking, the dorm also had a bigger kitchen that you could borrow the key to at the reception. My flat/kitchen had a microwave and kettle from prior tenants, but it really depends on the room.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The dorms in general are super scuffed and old, which is something to be aware of to not be shocked. I personally didn't mind too much, and living cost were super cheap and you will be living with other Erasmus students in the same boat. I was very happy staying in the dorms, despite the conditions. I would recommend bringing your own blanket or duvet to be a bit more comfy, it definitely made me feel more at home. Also whether or not the dorm had utensils, plates, kettle and so on depends on whether the prior tenants left something behind, so I would also recommend bringing your own utensils and kitchen towel.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is a minimarket at the dorm for essentials that has anything you might be suddenly missing, bread, noodles, milk, toilet paper, hygienic pads, covid test etc., but for bigger shopping the closest Lidl/Albert/DM is a bit further (closest is Centrum Stromovka) which is about 20 mins away. So I personally often went shopping after having been in the city for class.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had some issues at registration, that I really had to push to get fixed, but for most students you probably won't run into the same issues as I did.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Every faculty has a registration day, which is obligatory, and they tell you the process. It was a bit annoying however, that the regular students had already been able to register for courses before exchange students, so some courses were already full. Also at my faculty, we weren't able to get the login to register for courses until we got our student cards, so for me where the registration was double I wasn't able to register for classes until late.. And I know at some of the other faculties they got logins before their student cards, so they could register at the same time as the regular students..

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The most help you can get is if you just show up during office hours if it's kind of urgent. Your coordinator is pretty much the main person to help you, and if you're having issues it is their job to help you. Unfortunately my coordinator was a bit slow to help me with my registration problems, being persistent helps.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very, I was late to be able to sign up for courses, and since at my faculty we were already late to register as Erasmus my most wanted course from pre-approval was already full. In general you can still write the professors and ask for a spot even if the class is full, and waitlist to see if someone drops it until registration ends. Another problem was that the schedules were posted so late, so I didn't know until right before registration, that pretty much all the courses I had picked didn't match in the schedule, and therefore had to change almost my entire pre-approval.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't worry too much, you'll figure your courses out somehow. But also don't have your eyes set too much on specific courses, pick out more alternative options in case your combination of courses don't fit, so you won't be disappointed if the schedule doesn't fit.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: When looking at courses at Matfyz be aware of the grading. If it says 'C + Ex', it means you have to do both credit (C) as in assignments probably weekly, and an exam (Ex) to pass. The credit can also include a project in addition to the assignments. It is just something to keep in mind, with how much workload you will be taking on while on exchange. Having multiple classes with both credit and exam is a lot of work, depending on the difficulty of that course for you personally, and without my usual study group I found it difficult to manage. Just something to keep in mind.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In general course level is pretty similar to KU, but assignment workload feels like more at Matfyz at least, since you have more classes, and in my case, therefore more assignments weekly. Their method of teaching Computer Science specifically is also quite different to KU, in my experience at least. Their exams are also more of just remembering everything by heart, and to my experience always closed book.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lectures are pretty similar in structure. Some classes don't have practicals at all, and those that do is more of being in a smaller class with often a different teacher, where you sometimes do some exercises, but that usually isn't the main focus. In some ways similar, but feels more like working individually and then asking questions individually, and maybe going through some similar problems to the homework/assignment or prompts that practices for the exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Programming in C# (5 ECTS), 
Programming in Java (5 ECTS), 
Introduction to Machine Learning in Python (5 ECTS), 
Introduction to Computer Linguistics (3 ECTS), 
Data Science with R I (6 ECTS), 
Intensive Czech Language Course for Erasmus Students (7 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I highly recommend doing the Czech language course, even if your faculty won't approve the credits! You get a chance to meet other Erasmus students, learn some basic Czech and about Czech culture, and explore Prague all before the semester starts, highly highly recommend!
Also Data Science with R was probably my favourite course, I really liked the structure of having deadlines, but being able to do the course in my own pace (since lecture were pre-recorded).
If you find Machine Learning interesting it is of course a super useful course. It is a lot of work, so definitely find a good group from the beginning if you consider this course, otherwise you will most likely break your neck trying to pass the assignments, or loose a lot of your social life.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Generally everything is cheaper in Prague, and there weren't that many costs I didn't consider. When staying in the EU for more than 4 months without going home you might want to consider getting another SIM card to not get charged absurd fees on data. (That is what I did)
Also I spent a lot of money going out and going on a bunch of trips outside of Prague, which is definitely worth it!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transport is so cheap! I got two three-month student travel passes for 360 CZK each (about 112 DKK). 
In general most anything is cheaper, except the fish options are few since Czechia is not surrounded by water like Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are quite a few social organisations for Erasmus students. Both Erasmus in Prague, Oh My Prague, and my favourite ESN - Erasmus Student Network. Definitely good options to go meet other exchange students.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a few options at the faculties, but mainly I just used the Erasmus organisations.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to ESN events when you have time, it is a great place to meet other internationals, and also the organisers (usually Czechs) are usually super sweet.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to at least one of the ESN trips outside of Prague, you just need to sign up, it is generally a good deal, and they have an itinerary that you maybe wouldn't have come up with yourself. 
Explore as much outside of Prague as well, these are places you wouldn't usually get to see on a regular vacation, and the other cities also have a lot of charm.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, at times there definitely was a language barrier, but in general there was no issues as long as you're respectful.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Finding local friends can be kind of difficult since you're there temporarily, so the easiest way to find local friends is through the Buddy system, or befriending the ESN organisers. Regardless you might still find some nice local friends randomly at bars or in class.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Language was the main barrier, but was not a problem most of the time. If you have patience, a smile, and google translate you will have no issues culturally, most people are super sweet.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The beer is super cheap, and a big pride of Czechia. The city is also super well kept and you will never tire of looking at the pretty buildings and finding new culture gems.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be aware that you most likely will have to change your courses after arrival from your pre-approval.
2. Be open-minded, down to learn some basic Czech, and enjoy your time, it is a great opportunity.
3. I cannot recommend enough exploring outside of Prague!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is always good to have some cash on you, since even though most places take card you will probably run into a few places that don't, especially at bars. You won't have a problem using cash, since unlike Denmark a lot of places actually prefer cash.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The social life. Going to smaller cities, and making a bunch of international friends.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Courses, even getting to register for courses was a hassle, but I ended up struggling a lot with assignments because of my study group splitting up for Machine Learning. In my opinion, whether the course is credit + exam says more about the workload than the ECTS appointed the course. I would have liked a breakdown of how they calculate the credits for each course, since I don't think the workload is correctly taken into consideration for all the courses.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Despite everything, if you're even considering going on exchange, I would recommend just applying! How many times do you get an opportunity like this, and everything considered it is still completely worth it!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
